Evidence for a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid in the generalized Shastry-Sutherland model

Abstract

We present a multimethod investigation into the nature of the recently reported quantum spin liquid (QSL) phase in the spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. A comprehensive projective symmetry group classification of fermionic mean-field Ansätze on this lattice yields 46 U(1) and 80 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states. Using density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and exact diagonalization calculations, we find that the Shastry-Sutherland model and the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg antiferromagnet share the same QSL phase. Motivated by this observation, we establish an explicit mapping of our Ansätze to those on the square lattice, and identify the counterpart of the square-lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac QSL (Z2Az​zzz13) in the Shastry-Sutherland system. Employing state-of-the-art variational Monte Carlo calculations with Gutzwiller-projected wavefunctions, further improved by Lánczos steps, we demonstrate excellent agreement in both energies and correlation functions between a gapless (Dirac) ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid—characterized by only a few variational parameters—and results obtained from neural quantum states and DMRG. Working within a unified variational family that continuously connects the spin liquid to the adjacent Néel and plaquette valence-bond-crystal states, we locate the two phase boundaries in an unbiased way from the finite-size scaling of the respective order parameters and from correlation-ratio crossings, and find that both order parameters vanish continuously. Finally, we apply the recently developed Keldysh formulation of the pseudo-fermion functional renormalization group to compute the dynamical spin structure factor. The resulting spectra exhibit features consistent with Dirac cones in the excitation spectrum, providing strong independent evidence for a Dirac QSL ground state. Our identification of a dd-wave pairing ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac QSL is consistent with recently observed signatures of QSL behavior in Pr2Ga2BeO7 and makes predictions for future experiments.

I Introduction

The celebrated spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice presents a rare example of a two-dimensional spin model that admits an exact solution for its ground state [112]. This Archimedean lattice, which is also called the snub square or (32,4,3,4)(3^{2},4,3,4) lattice, features two symmetry-inequivalent bonds, and the Shastry-Sutherland model (SSM) is defined on this lattice as

H^=Js​∑⟨i,j⟩square𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+Jd​∑⟨i,j⟩dimer𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j.\hat{H}=J_{s}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle_{\rm square}}\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}+J_{d}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle_{\rm dimer}}\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}\,. (1)

Here, 𝐒^i\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i} denotes the SU(2) spin operator acting on the spin S= 1/2S\,{=}\,1/2 representation at site ii. The nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic exchange is given by JsJ_{s}, with the first sum in Eq. (1) running over all the bonds of the square lattice. The next-nearest-neighbor interaction is represented by JdJ_{d} and the second sum runs over the additional diagonal bonds introduced on every other plaquette of the square lattice, creating a pattern of alternating dimers [see Fig. 1(b)]. In the limit Js/Jd=0J_{s}/J_{d}=0, the Hamiltonian reduces to one consisting of decoupled dimers and the ground state is given by a tensor product of singlets with an energy of −3/8Jd-3/8\,J_{d} per site. This state is always an exact eigenstate of Eq. (1) and remains the ground state up to a finite critical Js/JdJ_{s}/J_{d}. The opposite limit, Js/Jd→∞J_{s}/J_{d}\to\infty, yields the Heisenberg model on the square lattice, which has a two-sublattice Néel-ordered ground state.

Over the past few decades, the SSM has been the focus of extensive theoretical efforts to map out the phase diagram of Eq. (1), with interest intensifying in particular after the discovery of SrCu2(BO3)2 [46, 81], which is well approximated by this model11 1 The role of interlayer couplings in accurately describing its behavior has lately been appreciated [116].. Other intriguing compounds in the family of Shastry-Sutherland lattice materials have also attracted much attention lately owing to their promise of hosting exotic nonmagnetic ground states, possibly QSLs, as well as exciting possibilities of realizing altermagnetism [28]. These include rare-earth magnets such as BaCe2ZnS5 [73], Pr2Ga2BeO7 [57], Pr2Be2GeO7 [58], Yb2Be2GeO7 [95], Er2Be2SiO7 [10], and Er2Be2GeO7 [126, 94].

With regard to the ground-state phase diagram of Eq. (1), while most early works advocated for a direct transition between the dimer and Néel phases [80, 121, 86], one of the first studies based on Schwinger-boson mean-field theory [4], and subsequent variational calculations [87], found an intermediate state with helimagnetic order, which is known to be the classical (S→∞)(S\to\infty) ground state [112]. Later investigations based on series expansion, stochastic state selection [88], coupled-cluster [22], and perturbative [50, 3] methods introduced the possibility of a gapped nonmagnetic intermediate phase, with either plaquette [52, 113] or columnar [137] valence-bond-crystal (VBC) order. The presence of plaquette order was subsequently confirmed by a large-NN expansion based on a generalization to S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N) symmetry [19], exact diagonalization and a combination of dimer- and quadrumer-boson methods [54], triplon mean-field analysis [53], two-step density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [83], and DD == 22 projected entangled pair states [44]. More recently, numerical quantum many-body approaches using tensor networks [20], DMRG [56], and the pseudo-fermion functional renormalization group (pf-FRG) [47] have established the presence of a plaquette-ordered ground state.

Today, the existence of an intermediate plaquette-VBC phase between the dimer and Néel orders has found broad consensus. This VBC breaks reflection symmetry across the lines containing the JdJ_{d} bonds, implying a twofold degenerate ground state, and features resonating singlets on “empty” plaquettes (with no JdJ_{d} bonds). In SrCu2(BO3)2, a plaquette VBC, likely ascribed to broken fourfold rotation symmetry about the centers of the empty squares, has been realized under the application of hydrostatic pressure [117, 136]. Thermodynamic measurements under high pressure have also provided evidence for the exciting possibility of a deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) between Néel order and the plaquette VBC [32]. Theoretical evidence for a continuous transition between the plaquette VBC and Néel-ordered states, and a resultant DQCP exhibiting emergent O(4) symmetry, has been provided by a combination of infinite density-matrix renormalization group (iDMRG) calculations and field-theoretic analysis [56], as well as recent tensor-network studies [65]. Other works have argued for a weak first-order transition between these phases [96, 12, 133, 72] and suggested that the DQCP might instead be proximate in parameter space [96, 125]. A recent field-theoretic study [29] by some of us formulated a fermionic gauge theory for the transition, characterizing it as a pseudocritical point with emergent SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry that naturally accommodates a gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid between the adjacent VBC and Néel phases.

In contrast to both of these scenarios, recent numerical investigations using DMRG [131], exact diagonalization [120, 89, 102], pf-FRG [47], and state-of-the-art neural-network quantum states [115, 79] have all reported the presence of a QSL phase sandwiched between the plaquette VBC and Néel-ordered states. This QSL phase occupies a narrow parameter range, 0.77≲Js/Jd≲0.820.77\lesssim J_{s}/J_{d}\lesssim 0.82 [131, 115]. This raises the question of whether one can (i) explore an extended parameter space to widen the window of QSL behavior, and (ii) identify its precise microscopic character, i.e., whether it is gapped or gapless, as well as the nature of its low-energy gauge group.

In this work, using a combination of DMRG and exact diagonalization calculations, we demonstrate that a broader “river” of spin liquidity can be accessed by activating antiferromagnetic exchange couplings on all the “other” diagonal bonds (within the square plaquettes) that were originally excluded in the Shastry-Sutherland geometry. As the strength of these additional interactions is increased, we observe no signs of a phase transition all the way to the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} limit. This suggests the intriguing possibility that the quantum spin liquids realized in the two models are adiabatically connected and therefore belong to the same quantum phase. Our analysis rigorously establishes this continuity using both numerical diagnostics and the framework of projective symmetry groups (PSGs). Unlike conventional ordered phases, which are characterized by spontaneous symmetry breaking and local order parameters, quantum spin liquids exhibit a more subtle form of organization known as “quantum order.” In this case, global symmetries are preserved, but they are implemented projectively on emergent fractionalized excitations such as spinons. This projective symmetry structure, captured systematically by the PSG classification, determines the allowed operators in the low-energy gauge theory and thereby fixes the universality class of the spin liquid.

Quantifying the width of the spin-liquid regime, we find that not only does it extend continuously from the square lattice to the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, but it also retains a finite extent in the parameter space of the latter, thus yielding new evidence for a robust QSL phase in the SSM. We find that the shared phase is a gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac quantum spin liquid, characterized by linearly dispersing spinon excitations at symmetry-protected Dirac nodes and an emergent gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field. Physically, such a state exhibits algebraically decaying spin correlations, broad continuum features in the dynamical structure factor rather than sharp magnon modes, and fractionalized spin-1/21/2 quasiparticles as its elementary excitations.

Importantly, the PSG construction does not merely enumerate symmetric parton Ansätze; as mentioned above, it determines how lattice symmetries act projectively on fractionalized spinons and thereby fixes the symmetry-allowed structure of the emergent gauge theory. Within this framework, the Dirac spin liquid naturally emerges as a parent state from which Néel and VBC phases can be obtained via Higgs instabilities, placing the Shastry-Sutherland and square-lattice models within a unified description of fermionic deconfined criticality.

II Connection to the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model

Previous studies using variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [34, 25], many-variable VMC [82], neural-network wavefunctions [90], DMRG [119], and tensor networks [63, 64] have offered evidence for the presence of a gapless spin liquid sandwiched between the Néel and VBC phases in the S=1/2S=1/2 square-lattice Heisenberg model with nearest-neighbor (J1J_{1}) and next-nearest-neighbor (J2J_{2}) couplings. On the other hand, as noted above, numerical simulations on the JsJ_{s}–JdJ_{d} SSM point to a variety of possibilities, including weakly first-order or continuous phase transitions or a gapless QSL phase. Given the geometric similarity between these two models, we introduce the following Hamiltonian that straightforwardly interpolates between them [96]:

H^\displaystyle\hat{H} =Js​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+Jd​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩dimer𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j\displaystyle=J_{s}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}+J_{d}\hskip-6.0pt\sum_{\langle\hskip-1.0pt\langle i,j\rangle\hskip-1.0pt\rangle_{\textrm{dimer}}}\hskip-6.0pt\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}
+J′d∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩orthogonal𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+J□∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩other𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j.\displaystyle+J^{\prime}_{d}\hskip-6.0pt\sum_{\langle\hskip-1.0pt\langle i,j\rangle\hskip-1.0pt\rangle_{\textrm{orthogonal}}}\hskip-6.0pt\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}+J_{\square}\hskip-6.0pt\sum_{\langle\hskip-1.0pt\langle i,j\rangle\hskip-1.0pt\rangle_{\textrm{other}}}\hskip-6.0pt\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}\,. (2)

These couplings are depicted in Fig. 1(c). In addition to the standard nearest-neighbor and dimer interactions of the SSM, denoted by JsJ_{s} and JdJ_{d}, respectively, we introduce two additional exchange couplings. Specifically, Jd′J^{\prime}_{d} labels the interactions on dimers that are orthogonal to those present in the original Shastry-Sutherland lattice, while J□J_{\square} denotes the interactions on the square plaquettes that are vacant in the SSM.

With these definitions, the limit Jd′=J□=0J^{\prime}_{d}=J_{\square}=0 reduces to the SSM, whereas the isotropic limit Jd′=Jd=J□J^{\prime}_{d}=J_{d}=J_{\square} corresponds to the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model. In the following, to interpolate continuously between the Shastry-Sutherland and square-lattice geometries, we vary a single tuning parameter defined as 𝒥≡Jd′=J□\mathcal{J}\equiv J^{\prime}_{d}=J_{\square}.

II.1 Density-matrix renormalization group

In Fig. 1, we illustrate the schematic phase diagram for this Hamiltonian, where the approximate phase boundaries are obtained from iDMRG simulations on an infinite cylinder with a circumference of L= 10L\,{=}\,10 and a bond dimension χ= 2000\chi\,{=}\,2000. In the hatched white region—which is studied more thoroughly in the next subsection—the simulation converges very slowly (or not at all, to within the conventionally accepted truncation error of 10−510^{-5}), with Néel and VBC order parameters that are both small and of similar magnitude. Furthermore, along the transverse direction indicated by the arrow in Fig. 1, we find no signatures of any phase transitions. This suggests that if a gapless spin-liquid phase exists in the SSM as proposed in Refs. [131, 115], it should be adiabatically connected to the gapless spin-liquid phase of the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model. For the chosen bond dimension, the phase transition between the VBC and Néel phases in the SSM appears to be weakly first-order.

In the following sections, we provide extensive evidence for this spin-liquid phase in the SSM based on exact diagonalization numerics.

II.2 Exact diagonalization

II.2.1 Low-energy levels and level spectroscopy

Long-range order in quantum many-body systems is characterized by the spontaneous breaking of a symmetry, manifested in nonvanishing correlation functions of the corresponding order parameters at large distances. Detecting such correlations reliably requires large system sizes, which are beyond the reach of exact diagonalization. However, a symmetry-broken phase is characterized not only by long-range correlations but also by a particular structure of low-energy states: in the thermodynamic limit, symmetry breaking implies a degenerate ground-state manifold, while on finite clusters, this degeneracy is lifted into a set of low-lying states distinguished by symmetry quantum numbers. Appropriate linear combinations of these states form the symmetry-broken ground states. Exact diagonalization excels at computing symmetry-resolved low-energy spectra for small clusters and is ideal for detecting signatures of symmetry breaking.

A paradigmatic example is the Néel antiferromagnet, which breaks SU(2) spin-rotation symmetry. Its finite-size spectrum exhibits the Anderson tower of states: the lowest states in each total-spin sector S=0,1,2,…S=0,1,2,\dots form a rotor spectrum with excitation energies scaling approximately as S⁡(S+1)/NS(S+1)/N, as illustrated in Fig. 2. These states are well separated from other excitations and have known quantum numbers, making the Anderson tower a robust diagnostic of magnetic long-range order in exact diagonalization studies.

Another example is the plaquette-singlet phase of the SSM, which breaks lattice symmetries. The ground-state manifold consists of two quasidegenerate singlets, denoted S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}, distinguished by lattice quantum numbers. The lowest magnetic excitation is a triplet T1T_{1}, followed by a second triplet T2T_{2} related to S2S_{2}, and a quintuplet Q1Q_{1}; here and below, T2T_{2} is specified by its symmetry quantum numbers (Table 1) and is in general not the second-lowest triplet in energy.

Phase transitions between competing orders can therefore be detected via level crossings in the low-energy spectrum. In particular, one of the singlet states (S1S_{1}) is common to both the Néel and plaquette phases, while the relative ordering of the second singlet associated with plaquette order and the lowest triplet of the Anderson tower determines whether a Néel or a plaquette state is favored. Tracking these crossings and their finite-size scaling provides a controlled method for locating phase boundaries.

While such level crossings are sufficient to identify transitions into magnetically or lattice-ordered phases, the identification of an intermediate quantum-disordered phase requires additional care. In particular, one must distinguish the absence of order from finite-size artifacts in small clusters. A recent work by Wang et al. [120] introduced an improved level-spectroscopic framework for the SSM, demonstrating that composite gaps between excited states (e.g., δT=E⁡(T2)−E⁡(S2)\delta_{T}=E(T_{2})-E(S_{2}) or δQ=E⁡(Q1)−E⁡(T1)\delta_{Q}=E(Q_{1})-E(T_{1})) allow unusually precise identification of phase boundaries even on small periodic clusters.

In this work, we extend that framework to a family of Hamiltonians interpolating continuously between the Shastry-Sutherland and J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} limits. Crucially, all lattice and spin symmetries of the SSM are preserved throughout the interpolation, with an enlargement of symmetry occurring only at the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} point. This allows the same symmetry assignments and identification of low-energy states used in Ref. [120] to be applied uniformly across the full parameter space.

We focus on a small set of symmetry-resolved low-energy states that evolve continuously across all phases. In the Néel phase, the states S1S_{1}, T1T_{1}, and Q1Q_{1} become the lowest members of the Anderson tower, while S2S_{2} and T2T_{2} move to higher energies. Table 1 summarizes the symmetry quantum numbers of the relevant states. As all wallpaper-group and spin symmetries of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice are preserved along the interpolation, these labels remain valid across the entire parameter range, allowing unambiguous tracking of the evolution and crossings of low-energy states.

II.2.2 Symmetry-resolved spectra

Figures 3 and 4 show the symmetry-resolved low-energy spectra obtained from Lánczos exact diagonalization for clusters of NN == 3232 and NN == 3636 sites (see also App. A for corresponding data on N=20,24,28N=20,24,28, and 4040-site clusters), as the model is interpolated from the Shastry-Sutherland limit to the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model. The evolution of the states S1S_{1}, S2S_{2}, T1T_{1}, T2T_{2}, and Q1Q_{1} is shown explicitly, together with the level crossings separating the Néel, spin-liquid, and singlet-ordered regimes. In Fig. 4, the downward motion of the BoB_{o} (S3S_{3}) and BeB_{e} (S4S_{4}) singlets near the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} limit, together with S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}, signals the emergence on finite clusters of the quasidegenerate four-state manifold associated with columnar VBC order, marking the termination of the spin-liquid regime on the singlet-ordered side. In the high-symmetry J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} limit, these four singlets occur at momenta (0,0)(0,0) (×2\times 2), (π,0)(\pi,0), and (0,π)(0,\pi). This momentum structure is the finite-size fingerprint of columnar VBC order, distinguishing it from a plaquette VBC, which decomposes into a different set of lattice irreducible representations; see Table II of Ref. [97].

Our central result is the identification of an intermediate spin-liquid regime that separates the Néel phase from the space-group-symmetry-breaking singlet-ordered phases. Spectroscopically, within this regime we do not observe clear signatures of either SU(2) spin-rotation symmetry breaking—as inferred via the Anderson tower of states—or quasidegenerate singlet manifolds signaling plaquette or columnar order. Instead, the lowest singlet and triplet excitations evolve smoothly with system size, and the relevant conventional and composite gap crossings delimit a finite-width region in parameter space.

II.2.3 Composite gaps and the river of liquidity

To test the internal consistency of the spin-liquid regime, we next follow the evolution of the low-energy spectrum along paths contained entirely within this extended region.

In Fig. 6, the plotted quantity is the width of the spin-liquid window, 𝒲QSL≡(Jd/Js)c,2−(Jd/Js)c,1\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{QSL}}\equiv(J_{d}/J_{s})_{c,2}-(J_{d}/J_{s})_{c,1}, i.e., the separation in Jd/JsJ_{d}/J_{s} between the two crossing points delimiting the spin-liquid regime at fixed 𝒥/Js\mathcal{J}/J_{s} (we use 𝒲\mathcal{W} rather than Δ\Delta here so as not to confuse this width in coupling space with the excitation gaps Δ⁡(Si)\Delta(S_{i}), Δ⁡(Ti)\Delta(T_{i}), and Δ⁡(Q1)\Delta(Q_{1})), evaluated with either of the two composite-gap constructions indicated in the legend, Δ⁡(T1)−δQ\Delta(T_{1})-\delta_{Q} and Δ⁡(T1)−δT\Delta(T_{1})-\delta_{T}. Each panel quotes the coefficient of the 1/N1/N term for whichever of the two data sets follows the linear form over the accessible cluster sizes (cTc_{T} for 𝒥/Js≤0.3\mathcal{J}/J_{s}\leq 0.3 and cQc_{Q} at 𝒥/Js=0.4\mathcal{J}/J_{s}=0.4), together with the extrapolated width, to which both constructions converge within our resolution.

As the Hamiltonian is deformed from the Shastry-Sutherland limit toward the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model, these crossings flow continuously without qualitative reorganization, demonstrating adiabatic connectivity of the intermediate phase. The resulting spin-liquid region therefore forms a continuous river of liquidity along the boundary of the Néel phase (see Figs. 5 and 6), extending across the full interpolation and terminating naturally at the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} point.

On the opposite boundary, adjoining the plaquette-singlet phase of the SSM and the columnar dimer phase of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model, the dominant low-energy levels also evolve adiabatically. The only qualitative change is the gradual appearance of additional singlet states associated with the enlarged degeneracy of the columnar dimer phase. These states “creep in” from higher energies on finite clusters and do not signal a breakdown of adiabatic continuity of the liquid regime, but rather the onset of lattice-symmetry breaking.

The accuracy of composite level spectroscopy in the SSM was demonstrated by Wang et al. [120], and our work extends this framework to reveal an adiabatically connected spin-liquid regime extending across distinct frustrated lattices.

II.2.4 Wavefunction overlap

Figure 7 provides complementary evidence for the adiabatic connectivity identified above by showing the overlap between a representative spin-liquid ground state and the exact ground states across the space of exchange couplings as a density plot. A continuous region of large overlap traces the river of liquidity along the Néel boundary, confirming that the spin-liquid states are adiabatically connected across the interpolation pathway.

By combining symmetry-resolved level spectroscopy with wave-function overlap diagnostics, we demonstrate that the spin-liquid regime identified in the SSM extends adiabatically to the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} limit on the square lattice. This river of liquidity forms a continuous boundary between Néel order and lattice-symmetry-breaking singlet phases, providing a unified spectral picture of quantum disorder in frustrated square-lattice antiferromagnets.

II.3 Summary of theoretical approach and results

Before turning to the parton description, we summarize what the numerics of this section have established and outline the route taken in the rest of the paper. Infinite DMRG locates a window in which the simulations converge poorly and the Néel and plaquette-VBC order parameters are both small (Sec. II.1), and symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization resolves that window spectroscopically. Along the entire interpolation to the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model the low-energy levels evolve without qualitative reorganization, and within the intermediate regime neither an Anderson tower nor a quasidegenerate singlet manifold develops (Sec. II.2). The composite-gap crossings delimiting this regime extrapolate to a finite width in the thermodynamic limit at every value of 𝒥/Js\mathcal{J}/J_{s} studied (Fig. 6), and the wavefunction-overlap map of Fig. 7 independently traces the same connected region—the river of liquidity. What these diagnostics cannot supply is the microscopic identity of the state: its gauge structure, the nature of its excitations, and whether the two ends of the river realize one and the same phase. The remainder of the paper addresses this question.

To further shed light on the nature of the QSL in the SSM, we employ the framework of projective symmetry groups (PSGs) [122, 123], described in Sec. III.2 (and extensively utilized on many two- and three-dimensional lattices [118, 55, 17, 127, 68, 69, 128, 78, 9, 132, 70, 8, 37, 36, 71, 60, 45, 108, 103, 61, 16, 15, 105, 74, 11, 62, 109, 76, 75]), to perform a systematic classification of fermionic mean-field states with SU(2), U(1), and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} low-energy gauge groups. Since previous studies [131, 115] have provided evidence for a gapless spin liquid, we choose to employ the fermionic representation of spin operators, as opposed to the bosonic one, because the former enables a description of gapless QSLs while the latter is restricted to describing only gapped QSLs [62]. Considering QSLs which respect the full space-group symmetry as well as QSLs compatible with the lower symmetry of the adjacent plaquette VBC, we present the microscopic Ansätze describing these states in Sec. IV. The classification yields 46 U(1) and 80 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG classes for the p​4​gp4g wallpaper group of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice; restricting the mean-field amplitudes to NN and NNN bonds leaves twelve U(1) and eighteen ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze (Fig. 9 and Table 4), while the reduced symmetry of the plaquette VBC—C4C_{4} preserved, GxG_{x} and σx​y\sigma_{xy} broken—admits a further 48 short-range ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze (App. H). Then, we develop a mapping between the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze on the Shastry-Sutherland and square lattices by establishing a connection between the PSGs of the respective symmetry groups. Adjoining the reflection σx\sigma_{x} enlarges p​4​gp4g to the square-lattice group p​4​mp4m and reproduces the 272 PSGs of Ref. [122]; the correspondence is established for six square-lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze in all (Table 6). This approach allows us to systematically narrow down the candidate wavefunctions for the potential QSL in the generalized SSM by identifying the parton Ansätze that can be adiabatically connected to those of the QSL phase in the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model.

In Sec. IV.3, we analyze the Ansatz on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice that maps to the Z2Az​zzz13 state on the square lattice: a gapless (Dirac) ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL, which is believed to provide an excellent variational description of the QSL in the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} square-lattice Heisenberg model [34, 90]. To characterize this Ansatz, we analyze its spinon band structure and compute the mean-field dynamical and equal-time spin structure factors at Js/Jd=0.80J_{s}/J_{d}=0.80, which lies within the putative QSL phase [131, 120, 47, 115]. We identify the state to be a gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac quantum spin liquid with dd-wave pairing. Its Dirac cones imply linearly dispersing spinon excitations, leading to algebraically decaying spin correlations in real space. In the dynamical spin structure factor, the fractionalized spinon pairs produce broad continua rather than sharp magnon modes, with enhanced spectral weight near twice the Dirac energy and characteristic fountain-like features emerging from the nodal points. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} nature of the state reflects the gapping out of gauge fluctuations by pairing, leaving gapless fermionic quasiparticles coupled to a gapped gauge sector.

As the spinon band structure is what most directly distinguishes the Shastry-Sutherland realization from its square-lattice counterpart, it is worth setting out the relation between the two here. The parent U(1) state with uniform real hopping has a Fermi surface at half filling; adding the nearest-neighbor dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} pairing Δs\Delta_{s} gaps it down to four Dirac points pinned at M(±π/2,±π/2)M(\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi/2), the IGG still being U(1). The empty-square pairing Δ□\Delta_{\square} then Higgses the gauge structure down to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, but leaves the nodes exactly where they are; their displacement along Γ​M¯\overline{\Gamma M} by ε\varepsilon is produced instead by the amplitudes that the lower p​4​gp4g symmetry permits, namely the diagonal hoppings χd\chi_{d}, χd′\chi_{d^{\prime}}, χ□\chi_{\square} and the chemical potential μ\mu 22 2 At Js/JdJ_{s}/J_{d} == 0.80.8 on a 14×1414\times 14 cluster, the optimized Ansatz gives ε=0.091\varepsilon=0.091 rad, i.e., ε≈0.029​π\varepsilon\approx 0.029\,\pi; the displacement is obtained in closed form in App. G, and its evolution with system size is listed in Table 15. The corresponding incommensurability of the gapless two-spinon momenta is δ=2​ε≈0.058​π\delta=2\varepsilon\approx 0.058\,\pi. In the Z2Az​zzz13 state, the Dirac cone splits into four cones at (π/2±ε,π/2±ε)(\pi/2\pm\varepsilon,\pi/2\pm\varepsilon) due to the dx​yd_{xy} pairing on the diagonal bonds connecting site (0,0)(0,0) to (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1), whereas if we introduce the dx​yd_{xy} pairing on the (±2,±2)(\pm 2,\pm 2) bonds, the Dirac cones remain intact at (π/2,π/2)(\pi/2,\pi/2).. In App. G, we reduce the nodal condition to a quartic polynomial whose coefficients are explicit functions of the mean-field amplitudes and solve it in closed form: the nodes stay exactly commensurate if and only if μ=±(χd+χd′−2​χ□)\mu=\pm(\chi_{d}+\chi_{d^{\prime}}-2\chi_{\square}), independently of both pairings. Evaluated on the optimized amplitudes, ε\varepsilon decreases monotonically with cluster size—from 0.078​π0.078\,\pi at L=6L=6 to 0.008​π0.008\,\pi at L=60L=60—following ε⁡(L)≃1.2/L+ε∞\varepsilon(L)\simeq 1.2/L+\varepsilon_{\infty} with ε∞≃0.002​π\varepsilon_{\infty}\simeq 0.002\,\pi (Table 15). The optimization thus drives the state toward this pinning manifold, so that the incommensurability δ=2​ε\delta=2\varepsilon of the gapless two-spinon momenta is a finite-size feature and the Shastry-Sutherland dispersion approaches that of the square-lattice Z2Az​zzz13 state in the thermodynamic limit.

In Sec. V, we carry out a state-of-the-art variational Monte Carlo study of the corresponding Gutzwiller-projected wavefunctions supplemented with Lánczos steps, and demonstrate the excellent agreement of the energies and equal-time correlators of our ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac QSL with those obtained from vision transformer (ViT) neural networks, DMRG, and exact diagonalization on small clusters. The projected Z3000 state attains the lowest energy of all the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze on every cluster from L=6L=6 to 4040, its pairing amplitudes Δs\Delta_{s} and Δ□\Delta_{\square} converge to finite values by L≃50L\simeq 50, and the empty-square pairing responsible for the Higgsing yields an energy gain of order 1%1\% over the parent U(1) state—evidence of a robust ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge structure in the thermodynamic limit. After two Lánczos steps and a zero-variance extrapolation, the energy per site at Js/Jd=0.80J_{s}/J_{d}=0.80 is E∞2​D/Jd=−0.4481​(3)E^{\rm 2D}_{\infty}/J_{d}=-0.4481(3), equal within error bars to the ViT and DMRG values but obtained with only eight variational parameters.

The correlation functions furnish the sharper test, and they also show how the state evolves along the river. On the 14×1414\times 14 cluster, the projected state reproduces the sign of every ViT correlator with quantitatively matching magnitudes, and its equal-time structure factor at the antiferromagnetic wavevector, 𝒮⁡(π,π)≈10.19\mathcal{S}(\pi,\pi)\approx 10.19, agrees with the ViT value of 9.899.89. The real-space spin-spin correlations decay algebraically with z+η=1.35​(3)z+\eta=1.35(3), consistent with the z+η=1.30​(3)z+\eta=1.30(3) obtained independently from the finite-size scaling of m2​(L)m^{2}(L), while the connected plaquette-plaquette correlations decay faster, with an exponent 1.62​(5)1.62(5). Such algebraic decay is a hallmark of gapless quantum spin liquids and is consistent with Dirac spinons coupled to a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field, whereas a gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state would give exponentially decaying correlations. Since the gauge structure is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, the exponent is not pinned to a universal value, and we verify explicitly that it varies smoothly along the river: the same analysis at the points marked in Figs. 6 and 7 gives z+η=1.29​(2)z+\eta=1.29(2), 1.40​(2)1.40(2), 1.48​(1)1.48(1), 1.60​(2)1.60(2), 1.74​(2)1.74(2), and 1.85​(2)1.85(2) for 𝒥/Js=0\mathcal{J}/J_{s}=0, 0.10.1, 0.20.2, 0.30.3, 0.40.4, and 0.50.5, respectively (Fig. 18). The evolution is monotonic and free of discontinuities, and it terminates inside the spread of values reported for the gapless QSL window of the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model, a range that is itself coupling dependent and on which the various methods do not agree. Band structure and correlation exponents therefore both interpolate continuously between the two limits, as expected if a single ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac phase spans the river.

Section VI then fixes the boundaries of this phase. The spin-liquid Ansatz is built from singlet hopping and pairing alone, so it cannot develop magnetic order by construction; we therefore embed it in a single variational family that treats the neighboring phases on the same footing, by adding an in-plane magnetic field to the spinon Hamiltonian (Sec. VI.1). Once both a transverse field and singlet pairing are present, no single-particle basis renders the mean-field Hamiltonian number conserving, so the projected amplitudes become Pfaffians rather than determinants. The plaquette VBC is treated analogously through the P5A Ansatz, the symmetry-lowered descendant of Z3000 identified in App. H, which returns to the symmetric state when its symmetry-inequivalent amplitudes are set equal. Within this family, both order parameters vanish continuously and each correlation ratio shows a single crossing rather than the two-branch structure of a first-order transition, placing the boundaries at (Js/Jd)PVBC≃0.78(J_{s}/J_{d})_{\rm PVBC}\simeq 0.78 and (Js/Jd)N​e´​el≃0.82(J_{s}/J_{d})_{\rm N\acute{e}el}\simeq 0.82 (Sec. VI.2). The energetic competition of separately optimized trial states, used here only as a consistency check, gives ≈0.78\approx 0.78 and ≈0.83\approx 0.83 (Sec. VI.3); both determinations agree with the DMRG, ED, neural-network, and tensor-network estimates collected in Table 11.

Independently of any variational input, the recently developed Keldysh formulation of the pseudo-fermion functional renormalization group yields the hitherto unreported dynamical spin structure factor of this QSL directly on the real-frequency axis, avoiding analytic continuation, at T/Jd=0.1T/J_{d}=0.1 on a 9×99\times 9 lattice. It exhibits two lobes of maximal low-energy intensity flanking (π,π)(\pi,\pi), appreciable weight at (π,π)(\pi,\pi) itself, and a broad continuum—precisely the pattern expected from scattering between Dirac cones displaced from MM—from a correlator-based method that makes no assumption about the wavefunction or its symmetry.

Taken together, these results provide compelling evidence for a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac quantum spin-liquid phase in the generalized Shastry-Sutherland model. Moreover, the adiabatic continuity established numerically between the Shastry-Sutherland and square-lattice limits indicates that both systems realize the same universal Dirac spin-liquid fixed point, rather than distinct lattice-specific phases. The river of liquidity therefore reflects a shared underlying infrared gauge theory. We emphasize that the projective realizations of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice symmetries are already built into the Ansätze and dictate their sign and amplitude structure. Hence, such an approach requires a much smaller number of variational parameters as compared to methods based on neural-network wavefunctions, DMRG, and many-variable VMC that rely on unconstrained optimizations.

In light of recent observations of gapless QSL behavior in Pr2Ga2BeO7 [57], which can approximately be modeled by S=1/2S=1/2 XXZ interactions on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, our results find additional significance. In particular, our finding of a dd-wave pairing ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac QSL is compatible with the thermodynamic signatures of a T2T^{2} dependence of the specific heat and a finite κ0/T\kappa_{0}/T arising from a disorder-induced finite density of states [57]. Taken together with indications from Keldysh pf-FRG of the persistent signatures of Dirac cones upon introduction of XXZ anisotropy to the Heisenberg model, our work supports the scenario of a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac QSL, thereby clarifying the microscopic identity of the QSL in Pr2Ga2BeO7.

III Methodology

III.1 Parton construction

A powerful framework to construct mean-field theories of QSLs is provided by the “parton” representation of spin operators. The first step in this scheme is to express the spin operators S^γ\hat{S}^{\gamma} (γ=x,y,z\gamma=x,y,z) in terms of spin-1/21/2, charge-neutral quasiparticles called spinons, which can be chosen to have either bosonic or fermionic statistics. As we are interested in describing gapped as well as gapless QSLs and the competition between them, we henceforth consider the spinons to be fermionic. In this language, the spin operator can be rewritten as a bilinear with two flavors of complex fermions [1, 5]:

S^iγ=12​∑α​βf^i​α†​τα​βγ​f^i​β.\displaystyle\hat{S}^{\gamma}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\beta}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}\tau^{\gamma}_{\alpha\beta}\hat{f}_{i\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}. (3)

Here, the f^i​α\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\alpha} (f^i​α†\hat{f}_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}) are spinon operators which annihilate (create) a spin-1/21/2 fermion with flavor α∈{↑,↓}\alpha\in\left\{\uparrow,\downarrow\right\} at site ii and τγ\tau^{\gamma} (γ=x,y,z\gamma=x,y,z) are the three Pauli matrices. In order to make the symmetries of the fermionic representation manifest, it proves instructive to re-express Eq. (3) as

S^iγ=14​Tr​[ψ^i†​τγ​ψ^i]\hat{S}^{\gamma}_{i}=\frac{1}{4}\text{Tr}\left[\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\tau^{\gamma}\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\right] (4)

in terms of the spinor doublet ψ^i\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i} ≡\equiv (f^i,f¯^i)(\hat{\textbf{f}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i},\hat{\bar{\textbf{f}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}), where f^i=(f^i,↑,f^i,↓)T\hat{\textbf{f}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}=(\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\uparrow},\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\downarrow})^{\mathrm{T}} and f¯^i=(f^i,↓†,−f^i,↑†)T\hat{\bar{\textbf{f}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}=(\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i,\downarrow},-\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i,\uparrow})^{\mathrm{T}}. Under a right multiplication ψ^i→ψ^i​Wi\hat{\psi}_{i}\rightarrow\hat{\psi}_{i}W_{i} with Wi∈W_{i}\in SU(2), the spin operators in Eq. (4) and the fermionic anticommutation relations of the spinons remain unaffected, i.e., such a transformation does not affect the physical observables. Thus, the fermionization of the spin operators is accompanied by a local gauge freedom associated with an internal symmetry group (ISG) [2, 66], which, in this case, is SU(2). In contrast to right multiplications, a left SU(2) multiplication, i.e., ψ^i→G​ψ^i\hat{\psi}_{i}\rightarrow G\hat{\psi}_{i} effects a rotation in spin space. Moreover, it is important to note that the on-site fermionic Hilbert space is ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4} while the spin space is ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. This necessitates the introduction of an additional constraint requiring that there be exactly one fermion per site:

ψ^i​τγ​ψ^i†=0,γ∈{x,y,z},\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\tau^{\gamma}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}=0,\;\gamma\in\{x,y,z\}, (5)

which ensures that the Hilbert space dimensions of the spin and spinon representations are in agreement.

Inserting Eq. (3) into a generic Heisenberg model such as, say, Eq. (1), yields a four-fermion interaction term in the Hamiltonian, following which we can perform a mean-field decoupling to obtain an effective quadratic Hamiltonian. Given that we intend to formulate a low-energy Hamiltonian for a spin-rotation-invariant quantum paramagnet, we restrict this decoupling to only the singlet channel. Since a spin rotation is implemented in the fermionic Hilbert space by a left SU(2) multiplication, the quadratic field ψ^i†​ψ^j\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j} is manifestly spin-rotation invariant. Accordingly, the mean field in the singlet channel can be identified as ui​j=⟨ψ^i†​ψ^j⟩u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}=\langle\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle, which, in turn, consists of two subchannels χi​j\chi_{ij} and Δi​j\Delta_{ij}:

ui​j=[χi​jΔi​j†Δi​j−χi​j†].\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}=\begin{bmatrix}{\chi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}&{\Delta}^{\dagger}_{ij}\\ {\Delta}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}&-{\chi}^{\dagger}_{ij}\end{bmatrix}. (6)

Here, χi​j\chi_{ij} and Δi​j\Delta_{ij} are the hopping and pairing singlet mean fields, respectively, which reside on the bond connecting sites ii and jj. The resulting quadratic spinon Hamiltonian for a quantum paramagnet generically takes the form

H^MF=\displaystyle\hat{H}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{MF}}= ∑⟨i​j⟩38​Ji​j​[12​Tr​(ui​j†​ui​j)+Tr​(ψ^i​ui​j​ψ^j†+H.c.)]\displaystyle\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\frac{3}{8}J^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\left[\frac{1}{2}\text{Tr}(u_{ij}^{\dagger}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij})+\text{Tr}(\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{j}+\text{H.c.})\right]\;
+∑i∑γaγ,iTr[ψ^iτγψ^i†].\displaystyle+\sum_{i}\sum_{\gamma}a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\gamma,i}\text{Tr}\left[\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\tau^{\gamma}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\right].\; (7)

The term in the second line above incorporates the constraint forbidding empty and doubly occupied sites at the mean-field level, i.e., ⟨ψ^i​τγ​ψ^i†⟩=0\langle\hat{\psi}_{i}\tau^{\gamma}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\rangle=0, using three Lagrange multipliers aγa_{\gamma}, with γ=x,y,z\gamma=x,y,z, at each site. As the spinon Hamiltonian is completely specified by (ui​j,aγ,iu_{ij},a_{\gamma,i}), these fields together constitute an Ansatz for a given QSL phase. The mean-field Hamiltonian (7) is now invariant under the following gauge transformations:

ψ^i→ψ^i​Wi,ui​j→Wi†​ui​j​Wj,aγ,i​τγ→aγ,i​Wi†​τγ​Wi,\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\rightarrow\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i},\;u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\rightarrow W^{\dagger}_{i}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j},\;a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\gamma,i}\tau^{\gamma}\rightarrow a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\gamma,i}W^{\dagger}_{i}\tau^{\gamma}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}, (8)

for Wi∈W_{i}\in SU(2). Therefore, the ISG turns out to also be the gauge-symmetry group in the mean-field construction. Next, we describe how this property leads to nontrivial symmetry operations in the fermionic Hilbert space.

III.2 Projective symmetry group framework

Fully symmetric QSLs are quantum paramagnets that do not spontaneously break lattice space-group and time-reversal symmetries and, consequently, cannot be characterized by local physical order parameters. In principle, QSLs may break one or more lattice symmetries and time reversal, but they still cannot be uniquely characterized by local order parameters since there can exist a plethora of QSLs breaking the very same symmetries—as occurs for chiral QSLs [8] and spin-/lattice-nematic QSLs [107, 99, 70]. To establish the invariance of an Ansatz under different symmetry operations, one therefore has to specify how a lattice or time-reversal symmetry operation acts in the fermionic Hilbert space.

In general, an Ansatz given by ui​ju_{ij} is modified to ui​j′u^{\prime}_{ij} == u𝒪⁡(i),𝒪⁡(j)u_{\mathcal{O}(i),\mathcal{O}(j)} under a symmetry operation denoted by 𝒪\mathcal{O}, so, at first sight, it appears that the symmetry of the Ansatz under 𝒪\mathcal{O} is broken. However, the SU(2) gauge symmetry in the fermionic representation implies that two Ansätze related by an SU(2) gauge transformation label the same physical spin state. Thus, if we choose an appropriate local SU(2) matrix WiW^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i} that connects ui​ju_{ij} and ui​j′u^{\prime}_{ij}, the symmetry of the Ansatz can be restored. As a result, lattice and time-reversal symmetries are realized projectively (i.e., up to SU(2) gauge transformations) in the fermionic Hilbert space. This lays the foundation for the idea of the projective symmetry group (PSG) framework [122], whereby an Ansatz is invariant under a symmetry operation 𝒪\mathcal{O} iff the following condition is satisfied:

W𝒪†​(𝒪⁡(i))​u𝒪⁡(i)​𝒪​(j)​W𝒪​(𝒪⁡(j))=ui​j.\displaystyle W^{\dagger}_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}(i))u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}(i)\mathcal{O}(j)}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}(j))=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}. (9)

This combined operation of the physical symmetry element and the element of the ISG defines the PSG of an Ansatz. Physically, if two Ansätze have gauge-inequivalent PSGs, they correspond to two distinct QSL states. Accordingly, PSGs serve to characterize the internal quantum order of an Ansatz [123], i.e., different Ansätze can be distinguished and characterized by PSGs in a fashion akin to how classical solid-state phases are characterized by crystallographic space-group symmetries. Hence, a systematic classification of projective representations of given lattice space groups can serve as a powerful mathematical tool, enabling the construction of distinct QSL Ansätze with a desired low-energy gauge group.

To characterize the Ansätze in more detail, note that ui​ju_{ij} in Eq. (6) can be re-expressed in terms of four real parameters as

ui​j=ι˙​χi​j0​τ0+χi​j3​τz+Δi​j1​τx+Δi​j2​τy,u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{ij}\tau^{0}+\chi^{3}_{ij}\tau^{z}+\Delta^{1}_{ij}\tau^{x}+\Delta^{2}_{ij}\tau^{y}, (10)

where τ0\tau^{0} is the 2×22\times 2 identity matrix, so that the two complex mean fields of Eq. (6) read χi​j=ι˙​χi​j0+χi​j3\chi_{ij}=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{ij}+\chi^{3}_{ij} and Δi​j=Δi​j1+ι˙​Δi​j2\Delta_{ij}=\Delta^{1}_{ij}+\dot{\iota}\Delta^{2}_{ij}. Due to this structure, there always exists a group 𝔾\mathbb{G} (where 𝔾\mathbb{G} is either SU(2) or its subgroups U(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}) such that under gauge transformations by 𝒢i∈𝔾\mathcal{G}_{i}\in\mathbb{G}, the Ansatz remains invariant. The group 𝔾\mathbb{G} is called the invariant gauge group (IGG) of the Ansatz. Another interpretation of the IGG can be seen by comparing Eqs. (9) and (11) below, which implies that the IGG is a special subgroup of the PSG corresponding to an identity symmetry operation (𝒪=𝟙\mathcal{O}=\mathds{1}).

When ui​ju_{ij} == ι˙​χi​j0​τ0\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{ij}\tau^{0}, and χi​j3\chi^{3}_{ij} == Δi​j1=Δi​j2\Delta^{1}_{ij}=\Delta^{2}_{ij} == 00, i.e., the Ansatz consists of only imaginary hoppings, the IGG is the global SU(2) gauge group {exp⁡(ι˙​ϕ​𝐧^⋅𝝉)}\{\exp({\dot{\iota}\phi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\bm{\tau}})\}. If we include real hopping terms as well, i.e., χi​j3≠0\chi^{3}_{ij}\neq 0 but Δi​j1=Δi​j2=0\Delta^{1}_{ij}=\Delta^{2}_{ij}=0, the IGG is the global U(1) gauge group {exp⁡(ι˙​ϕ​τz)}\{\exp({\dot{\iota}\phi\,\tau^{z}})\} while the inclusion of pairing terms breaks the IGG down to global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, {±1}\{\pm 1\}. The three different IGGs discussed in this example only involve global gauge elements; these correspond to the so-called canonical structures of the Ansätze. In canonical form, SU(2) Ansätze contain only imaginary hopping terms, U(1) Ansätze include only real and imaginary hopping amplitudes, and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze can take any generic form. However, owing to the SU(2) gauge redundancy, the elements of the IGG need not always constitute a global gauge group, and the invariance of an Ansatz may require the following generic local operation:

𝒢i†​ui​j​𝒢j=ui​j,𝒢∈IGG.\mathcal{G}_{i}^{\dagger}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\mathcal{G}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij},\;\mathcal{G}\in\mathrm{IGG}. (11)

Thus, in general, the IGG is a local gauge group.

III.3 Symmetries of the Shastry-Sutherland model

The symmetries of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice [see Fig. 1(b)] correspond to the p​4​gp4g wallpaper group. Let the positions of the lattice sites in the Cartesian coordinate system be denoted by

𝐫≡(x,y)≡(x​𝐱^+y​𝐲^)​a,\mathbf{r}\equiv(x,y)\equiv(x\mathbf{\hat{x}}+y\mathbf{\hat{y}})a, (12)

where aa is the lattice parameter. The symmetry generators and their actions on a lattice site are then as follows [56]:

Tx​(x,y)\displaystyle T_{x}(x,y) →(x+2,y),\displaystyle\rightarrow(x+2,y), (13)
Ty​(x,y)\displaystyle T_{y}(x,y) →(x,y+2),\displaystyle\rightarrow(x,y+2),
Gx​(x,y)\displaystyle G_{x}(x,y) →(x+1,−y),\displaystyle\rightarrow(x+1,-y),
Gy​(x,y)\displaystyle G_{y}(x,y) →(−x,y+1),\displaystyle\rightarrow(-x,y+1),
σx​y​(x,y)\displaystyle\sigma_{xy}(x,y) →(y,x),\displaystyle\rightarrow(y,x),
σx​y¯​(x,y)\displaystyle\sigma_{x\bar{y}}(x,y) →(−y+1,−x+1),\displaystyle\rightarrow(-y+1,-x+1),
C4​(x,y)\displaystyle C_{4}(x,y) →(−y+2,x−1).\displaystyle\rightarrow(-y+2,x-1).

Here, TxT_{x} and TyT_{y} stand for translations by 2​a​𝐱^2a\mathbf{\hat{x}} and 2​a​𝐲^2a\mathbf{\hat{y}}, respectively, on the underlying Bravais (square) lattice. The operation GxG_{x} (GyG_{y}) is a glide reflection that combines a translation a​𝐱^a\mathbf{\hat{x}} (a​𝐲^a\mathbf{\hat{y}}) with a reflection across the xx- (yy-) axis. The symmetries σx​y\sigma_{xy} and σx​y¯\sigma_{x\bar{y}} denote reflections across the two diagonal axes, while C4C_{4} represents fourfold rotations about the centers of the empty squares. Note that TxT_{x}, TyT_{y}, GyG_{y}, σx​y¯\sigma_{x\bar{y}}, and C4C_{4} can be expressed in terms of GxG_{x} and σx​y\sigma_{xy} as

Gy\displaystyle G_{y} =σx​y​Gx​σx​y,\displaystyle=\sigma_{xy}G_{x}\sigma_{xy}, (14)
Tx\displaystyle T_{x} =Gx2,Ty=Gy2,\displaystyle=G_{x}^{2},\quad T_{y}=G_{y}^{2},
σx​y¯\displaystyle\sigma_{x\bar{y}} =σx​y​Gx​Gy−1,\displaystyle=\sigma_{xy}G_{x}G_{y}^{-1},
C4\displaystyle C_{4} =Gx​σx​y​Gx​Gy−1=Gx​σx​y¯.\displaystyle=G_{x}\sigma_{xy}G_{x}G_{y}^{-1}=G_{x}\sigma_{x\bar{y}}.

Thus, GxG_{x} and σx​y\sigma_{xy} form a minimal set of symmetry generators for the p​4​gp4g wallpaper group. However, for simplicity, we include the translations TxT_{x} and TyT_{y} explicitly in the discussion hereafter.

Using the notation (m,n,u)(m,n,u), the position of a lattice site is expressed as

𝐫≡(r,u)≡(m,n,u)≡2​(m​𝐱^+n​𝐲^)​a+ϵu,\mathbf{r}\equiv(r,u)\equiv(m,n,u)\equiv 2(m\mathbf{\hat{x}}+n\mathbf{\hat{y}})a+\bm{\epsilon}_{u}, (15)

where u=1,2,3,4u=1,2,3,4 labels the four distinct sites within the geometric unit cell, and

ϵ1=0,ϵ2=a​𝐱^,ϵ3=a⁡(𝐱^+𝐲^),ϵ4=a​𝐲^.\bm{\epsilon}_{1}=0,\quad\bm{\epsilon}_{2}=a\mathbf{\hat{x}},\quad\bm{\epsilon}_{3}=a(\mathbf{\hat{x}}+\mathbf{\hat{y}}),\quad\bm{\epsilon}_{4}=a\mathbf{\hat{y}}. (16)

The symmetry operations, in this notation, are defined as

Tx:(m,n,u)\displaystyle T_{x}:(m,n,u) →(m+1,n,u),\displaystyle\rightarrow(m+1,n,u), (17)
Ty:(m,n,u)\displaystyle T_{y}:(m,n,u) →(m,n+1,u),\displaystyle\rightarrow(m,n+1,u),
Gx:(m,n,u)\displaystyle G_{x}:(m,n,u) →(m+δu,2/3,−n−δu,3/4,Gx​(u)),\displaystyle\rightarrow\big(m+\delta_{u,2/3},-n-\delta_{u,3/4},G_{x}(u)\big),
σx​y:(m,n,u)\displaystyle\sigma_{xy}:(m,n,u) →(n,m,σx​y​(u)),\displaystyle\rightarrow\big(n,m,\sigma_{xy}(u)\big),

where δu,a/b≡δu,a+δu,b\delta_{u,a/b}\equiv\delta_{u,a}+\delta_{u,b}, Gx​({1,2,3,4})={2,1,4,3}G_{x}(\{1,2,3,4\})=\{2,1,4,3\}, and σx​y​({1,2,3,4})={1,4,3,2}\sigma_{xy}(\{1,2,3,4\})=\{1,4,3,2\}.

In addition to the space-group symmetries, we need to consider time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} given that we are dealing with fully symmetric QSL Ansätze. Being an internal symmetry, 𝒯\mathcal{T} leaves (m,n,u)(m,n,u) unchanged and commutes with all space-group operations. Taking 𝒯\mathcal{T} into account, the symmetry group of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice is then fully specified by the following identity relations:

Tx−1​Ty−1​Tx​Ty\displaystyle T_{x}^{-1}T_{y}^{-1}T_{x}T_{y} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1}, (18)
Gx−1​Tx−1​Gx​Tx\displaystyle G_{x}^{-1}T_{x}^{-1}G_{x}T_{x} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
Gx−1​Ty​Gx​Ty\displaystyle G_{x}^{-1}T_{y}G_{x}T_{y} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
Tx−1​Gx2\displaystyle T_{x}^{-1}G_{x}^{2} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
Ty−1​σx​y−1​Tx​σx​y\displaystyle T_{y}^{-1}\sigma_{xy}^{-1}T_{x}\sigma_{xy} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
Tx−1​σx​y−1​Ty​σx​y\displaystyle T_{x}^{-1}\sigma_{xy}^{-1}T_{y}\sigma_{xy} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
(σx​y​Gx)4\displaystyle(\sigma_{xy}G_{x})^{4} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
σx​y2\displaystyle\sigma_{xy}^{2} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
𝒯2\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{2} =𝟙,\displaystyle=\mathds{1},
𝒯​𝒪​𝒯−1​𝒪−1\displaystyle\mathcal{T}\mathcal{O}\mathcal{T}^{-1}\mathcal{O}^{-1} =𝟙,𝒪∈{Tx,Ty,Gx,σx​y}.\displaystyle=\mathds{1},\quad\mathcal{O}\in\{T_{x},T_{y},G_{x},\sigma_{xy}\}.

Finally, time-reversal symmetry acts nontrivially on the mean fields, as 𝒯⁡(ui​j,aγ)=−(ui​j,aγ)\mathcal{T}(u_{ij},a_{\gamma})=-(u_{ij},a_{\gamma}) [122, 8]. This imposes the condition

W𝒯†​(i)​ui​j​W𝒯​(j)=−ui​j,W^{\dagger}_{\mathcal{T}}(i)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(j)=-u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}, (19)

where W𝒯∈W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}\in SU(2) is a site-dependent gauge transformation.

Since the physical symmetries act projectively in the fermionic Hilbert space, the group relations of Eq. (18), which are generically of the type

𝒪1∘𝒪2∘⋯=1,\mathcal{O}_{1}\circ\mathcal{O}_{2}\circ\cdots=1, (20)

naturally translate to gauge-enriched group compositions of the type

𝒪~1∘𝒪~2∘⋯=(W𝒪1∘𝒪1)∘(W𝒪2∘𝒪2)∘⋯=𝒢,\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{1}\circ\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{2}\circ\cdots=(W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}_{1}}\circ\mathcal{O}_{1})\circ(W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}_{2}}\circ\mathcal{O}_{2})\circ\cdots=\mathcal{G}, (21)

where 𝒢∈IGG\mathcal{G}\in{\rm IGG} is a pure gauge transformation which reduces to the identity operation for spins. The complete set of PSG solutions can be obtained using the relations in Eq. (18); the explicit gauge-enriched relations for the space group of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice are collected in App. B.

Let us first consider the case where the IGG is U(1). The generic form of a U(1) PSG solution for any symmetry operator 𝒪\mathcal{O}, in the canonical gauge, is given by W𝒪​(m,n,u)=F3​(ϕ𝒪​(m,n,u))​(ι˙​τx)w𝒪W_{\mathcal{O}}(m,n,u)=F_{3}(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}(m,n,u))(\dot{\iota}\tau^{x})^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}}, where F3​(λ)≡exp⁡(ι˙​λ​τz)F_{3}(\lambda)\equiv\exp({\dot{\iota}\lambda\tau^{z}}), and w𝒪w_{\mathcal{O}} takes the values 00 and 11. However, due to the consistency conditions on GxG_{x} arising from the relations (18), there exist no solutions with w𝒪=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}=1 for 𝒪∈{Tx,Ty}\mathcal{O}\in\{T_{x},T_{y}\}. The solutions for ϕ𝒪​(m,n,u)\phi_{\mathcal{O}}(m,n,u) can be written as

ϕTx​(m,n,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{x}}(m,n,u) =n​ξy,ϕTy​(m,n,u)=0,\displaystyle=n\,\xi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y},\;\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{y}}(m,n,u)=0, (22)
ϕGx​(m,n,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}}(m,n,u) =(−1)wGx​(n​ξGx​y+m​ξy​δu,3/4)+ϕ¯Gx,u,\displaystyle=(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}}}(n\,\xi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{xy}}+m\,\xi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}\delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{u,3/4})+\bar{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x},u}, (23)
ϕσx​y​(m,n,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{xy}}(m,n,u) =m​n​ξy+ϕ¯σx​y,u,\displaystyle=mn\,\xi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}+\bar{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{xy},u}, (24)
ϕ𝒯​(m,n,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(m,n,u) =u​π​δw𝒯,0,\displaystyle=u\pi\,\delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{w_{\mathcal{T}},0}, (25)

with ϕ¯𝒪,u\bar{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O},u} ≡\equiv ϕ𝒪​(0,0,u)\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}(0,0,u); for details, refer to App. C. The different gauge-inequivalent choices of the phases 0≤ξy0\leq\xi_{y}, ξGx​y\xi_{G_{xy}}, ϕ¯Gx,u\bar{\phi}_{G_{x},u}, ϕ¯σx​y,u<2​π\bar{\phi}_{\sigma_{xy},u}<2\pi are listed in Table 2. We find a total of 4646 U(1) solutions that can be realized on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice.

When the IGG is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, an identity can be defined up to a global sign in the canonical gauge. The solutions for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs (for details, see App. D) can be expressed as

WTx​(m,n,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{x}}(m,n,u) =WTy​(m,n,u)=τ0,\displaystyle=W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{y}}(m,n,u)=\tau^{0}\ ,\; (26)
WGx​(m,n,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}}(m,n,u) =ηGx​yn​𝒲Gx,u,\displaystyle=\eta^{n}_{G_{xy}}\mathcal{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x},u}\ ,\; (27)
Wσx​y​(m,n,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{xy}}(m,n,u) =𝒲σx​y,u,\displaystyle=\mathcal{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{xy},u}\ ,\; (28)
W𝒯​(m,n,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(m,n,u) =𝒲𝒯,u,\displaystyle=\mathcal{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}\,, (29)

where ηGx​y=±1\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{xy}}=\pm 1, and the matrices 𝒲𝒪,u=W𝒪​(0,0,u)\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{O},u}=W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}(0,0,u) can be read off from Table 3. While there are 24×5=802^{4}\times 5=80 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs in total, for the ηGx​𝒯=1\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}\mathcal{T}}=1 class—in the first and fifth rows of Table 3—every mean-field amplitude vanishes identically, since 𝒲𝒯,u∝τ0\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{T},u}\propto\tau^{0} on all four sublattices, so we need to consider only 6464 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSGs.

IV Mean-field Ansätze

Having worked out the complete set of PSGs for the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, we are now in a position to derive the different realizable symmetric mean-field Ansätze from these PSG solutions. Restricting the mean-field amplitudes to square-lattice bonds (nearest neighbor, NN) and diagonal bonds (next-nearest neighbor, NNN) only, we find a total of twelve distinct U(1) and eighteen ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze. In addition to their PSGs, all the Ansätze can be further characterized by defining SU(2) flux operators [8, 122], which are associated with different loops originating from a fixed base point ii:

P𝒞i\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{C}_{i}} =ui​juj​k⋯ul​i,\displaystyle=u_{ij}u_{jk}\cdots u_{li}, (30)

where j,k,l,…j,k,l,\ldots denote the sites included in the contour 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}. Under a local SU(2) gauge transformation W⁡(i)W(i), the flux operator transforms as P𝒞i→W†​(i)​P𝒞i​W​(i)P_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}\rightarrow W^{\dagger}(i)P_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}W(i), which affects all loop operators with the same base point only up to a global rotation in Pauli space. This property provides a powerful tool for diagnosing different QSL Ansätze. In general, for a qq-sided loop, P𝒞iP_{\mathcal{C}_{i}} takes the form

P𝒞i​(φ𝒞i)∝gi​eι˙​φ𝒞i​τz​(τz)q​gi†,gi∈SU⁡(2),P^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}(\varphi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}})\propto g^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}e^{\dot{\iota}\varphi_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}\tau^{z}}(\tau^{z})^{q}g_{i}^{\dagger},\quad g^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\in\mathrm{SU(2)}, (31)

where the phase φ𝒞i\varphi_{\mathcal{C}_{i}} can be interpreted as a magnetic flux threading the loop 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}.

Furthermore, note that the IGG of an Ansatz may not be obvious if the Ansatz is not in the canonical gauge. In that case, the disguised IGG for an Ansatz written in a generic gauge can be identified from the condition [8]:

[𝒢,P𝒞i]=0,[\mathcal{G},P_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}]=0,

for 𝒢∈IGG\mathcal{G}\in\text{IGG} and all nontrivial flux loops {P𝒞i}\{P_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}\}. In the context of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, starting from a base site at the origin, we identify four square loops and three triangular loops as illustrated in Fig. 8(a). The associated gauge fluxes are denoted by φs1\varphi_{s_{1}}, φs2\varphi_{s_{2}}, φs3\varphi_{s_{3}}, φs4\varphi_{s_{4}}, φt1\varphi_{t_{1}}, φt2\varphi_{t_{2}}, and φt3\varphi_{t_{3}}, respectively.

In the following, we discuss the QSL mean-field Ansätze for different IGGs. All these Ansätze are defined by simply considering the reference bonds shown in Fig. 8(b).

IV.1 U(1) Ansätze on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice

To begin, we consider the different Ansätze realizable with IGG U(1). In this family, we divide the U(1) PSG solutions into eight different classes, denoted as U1, U2, …\dots, U8, corresponding to the eight rows in Table 2. The states are labeled by their respective classes and the parameters of the PSG as “Class ​ξGx​y​ϕ¯σx​y\text{Class }\xi_{G_{xy}}\bar{\phi}_{\sigma_{xy}}”, where ϕ¯σx​y\bar{\phi}_{\sigma_{xy}} == pσx​y​πp_{\sigma_{xy}}\pi. The flux patterns of all the U(1) Ansätze are depicted in Fig. 9.

The class U1 yields four distinct Ansätze labeled as U100, U1π\pi0, U10π\pi, and U1π​π\pi\pi. Notably, for U10π\pi, the mean-field amplitudes on the diagonal bonds vanish due to symmetry, and a uniform π\pi-flux threads all the plaquettes, corresponding to a QSL with an SU(2) IGG realized on the square lattice [122].

Next, the four Ansätze, labeled as U300, U3π\pi0, U30π\pi, and U3π​π\pi\pi, belong to the class U3. The symmetry-allowed mean fields for U30π\pi and U3π​π\pi\pi are identical to those of U10π\pi and U1π​π\pi\pi, respectively. However, the U3 class has a staggered chemical potential, whereas the chemical potential is uniform for the U1 class. Both the U1 and U3 classes of Ansätze consist of real hopping terms only.

Additionally, we identify a few more classes of U(1) Ansätze, labeled as U500, U50π\pi, U600, U60π\pi, and U8ξ\xi0. In these cases, the mean-field amplitudes vanish on the diagonal bonds, as does the onsite potential, while the square bonds include both real and imaginary hopping terms. Note that for the U5 class Ansätze, a nontrivial flux, i.e., ≠0,π\neq 0,\pi, threads the empty squares of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, while for the U6 class a nontrivial flux threads those squares of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice which would have otherwise featured a diagonal bond. Up to NN bonds, these two classes of Ansätze are equivalent.

The U8ξ​0\xi 0 class (with ξ\xi ≡\equiv ξGx​y\xi_{G_{xy}}), in particular, incorporates a series of mean-field Ansätze. The explicit structure of the mean-field amplitudes in this case is given by

us\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s} =ι˙​χs0​τ0+χs3​τz=u12=−u14†=−u23\displaystyle=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{s}\tau^{0}+\chi^{3}_{s}\tau^{z}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{12}=-u^{\dagger}_{14}=-u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{23}
=u43†=−u21†=u41=F3​(ξ)​u32†=−F3​(ξ)​u34.\displaystyle=u^{\dagger}_{43}=-u^{\dagger}_{21}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{41}=F^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3}(\xi)u^{\dagger}_{32}=-F^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3}(\xi)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{34}. (32)

The bonds u41u_{41} and u32u_{32} are modified under a translation TxT_{x}, while all other bonds remain invariant:

u41​(m,n)=u(m,n,4),(m,n+1,1)=F3​(2​m​ξ)​u41,u32​(m,n)=u(m,n,3),(m,n+1,2)=F3​(2​m​ξ)​u32.\left.\begin{aligned} &u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{41}(m,n)=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{(m,n,4),(m,n+1,1)}=F^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3}(2m\xi)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{41},\\ &u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{32}(m,n)=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{(m,n,3),(m,n+1,2)}=F^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3}(2m\xi)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{32}.\end{aligned}\right. (33)

To realize such an Ansatz on a finite lattice, one must impose the constraint

ξ=ξGx​y=𝒫𝒬​π,with ​𝒫∈ℤ≥0,𝒬∈ℤ+.\xi=\xi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{xy}}=\frac{\mathcal{P}}{\mathcal{Q}}\pi,\quad\text{with }\mathcal{P}\in\mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0},\;\mathcal{Q}\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}. (34)

Thus, for each choice 𝒫/𝒬∈[0,1]\mathcal{P}/\mathcal{Q}\in[0,1], Eq. (34) provides a realization of at least one fully symmetric mean-field QSL within this PSG class, and in total, there exists an infinite number of such QSLs [122].

Lastly, we note that U(1) Ansätze in classes U2, U4, and U7 cannot be realized with the amplitudes restricted to NNN bonds.

IV.2 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice

Although there exist a total of 64 projective extensions of the symmetry group with IGG ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, only 18 of these can be realized when the Ansätze are restricted to NNN mean-field amplitudes. The symmetric ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze have the following structure:

us=ι˙​χs0​τ0+Δs1​τx+Δs2​τy+χs3​τz,\displaystyle u_{s}=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{s}\tau^{0}+\Delta^{1}_{s}\tau^{x}+\Delta^{2}_{s}\tau^{y}+\chi^{3}_{s}\tau^{z}, (35)
u12=ησ​u43†=ηGx​Tx​u21=ηGx​Tx​ησ​ηGx​y​u34†=us,\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{12}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma}u^{\dagger}_{43}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}T_{x}}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{21}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}T_{x}}\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma}\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{xy}}u^{\dagger}_{34}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}, (36)
u14=u23†=ηGx​Tx​u41=ηGx​Tx​ηGx​y​u32†=(τz)p​us​(τz)p,\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{14}=u^{\dagger}_{23}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}T_{x}}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{41}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{x}T_{x}}\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{G_{xy}}u^{\dagger}_{32}=(\tau^{z})^{p}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}(\tau^{z})^{p}, (37)
u13=u42=ud=ι˙​χd0​τ0+Δd1​τx+Δd2​τy+χd3​τz,\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{13}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{42}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{d}=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{d}\tau^{0}+\Delta^{1}_{d}\tau^{x}+\Delta^{2}_{d}\tau^{y}+\chi^{3}_{d}\tau^{z}, (38)
