here, p≡0​(1)p\equiv 0(1) for 𝒲σx​y,u\mathcal{W}_{\sigma_{xy},u} ∝\propto τ0​(z)\tau^{0(z)}. In the equations above, the sign parameter ηGx​Tx\eta_{G_{x}T_{x}} is irrelevant because, up to NNNs, Ansätze with positive and negative ηGx​Tx\eta_{G_{x}T_{x}} are related by a gauge transformation.

We label the Ansätze using the scheme

Z​PSGrow​(1−ηGx​y2)​(1−ησ2)​(1−ηGx​𝒯2),\text{Z}\;\text{PSG}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{1-\eta_{G_{xy}}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\eta_{\sigma}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\eta_{G_{x}\mathcal{T}}}{2}\right), (40)

where PSGrow\text{PSG}_{\text{row}} corresponds to the row number in Table 3.

Upon restricting ourselves to only JsJ_{s} and JdJ_{d} bonds, a total of 18 different symmetric Ansätze with IGG ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} can be realized—these are listed in Table 4. They are also graphically represented in Fig. 10(a), where the parameter ηGx​Tx\eta_{G_{x}T_{x}} is omitted for simplicity. However, this parameter does become important when establishing a connection of our PSGs with those on the square lattice, as discussed in the following section.

IV.3 Mapping to square-lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze

In this section, we show how the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL Ansätze on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice can be continuously connected to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze realizable on the square lattice [122].

The square lattice has a higher symmetry than the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The wallpaper group of the square lattice is p​4​mp4m, which is generated by two translations T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} by a​𝐱^a\mathbf{\hat{x}} and a​𝐲^a\mathbf{\hat{y}}, respectively, and three reflections σx​y\sigma_{xy}, σx\sigma_{x}, and σy\sigma_{y} about the x=yx=y, y=0y=0, and x=0x=0 lines, respectively. As we show here, including σx\sigma_{x} transforms the wallpaper group p​4​gp4g of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice into p​4​mp4m. The reflection σx\sigma_{x} transforms the coordinate (x,y)(x,y) to (x,−y)(x,-y) and acts on (m,n,u)(m,n,u) as

σx:(m,n,u)→(m,−n−δu,3/4,u).\sigma_{x}:(m,n,u)\rightarrow(m,-n-\delta_{u,3/4},u). (41)

One can verify that the other generators of the square lattice can be obtained as follows:

T1=Gx​σx,T2=σx​y​Gx​σx​σx​y=σx​y​T1​σx​y,σy=σx​y​σx​σx​y.\left.\begin{aligned} &T_{1}=G_{x}\sigma_{x},\\ &T_{2}=\sigma_{xy}G_{x}\sigma_{x}\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{xy}T_{1}\sigma_{xy},\\ &\sigma_{y}=\sigma_{xy}\sigma_{x}\sigma_{xy}.\end{aligned}\right. (42)

Hence, the wallpaper group p​4​mp4m is generated by {Gx,σx​y,σx}\{G_{x},\sigma_{xy},\sigma_{x}\}. Using this symmetry group, we establish a mapping from the Shastry-Sutherland lattice PSGs to the square-lattice PSGs in App. E. We find that upon including σx\sigma_{x}, the Ansätze belonging to the ηGx​y=−1\eta_{G_{xy}}=-1 class have to be excluded as we are incorporating a larger set of symmetries. Note that this class is also the one which yields (0,π,0,π)(0,\pi,0,\pi)- and (π,0,π,0)(\pi,0,\pi,0)-flux phases in the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, while such staggered-flux phases are forbidden on the square lattice [122]. In all, we arrive at the 272 PSGs found in Ref. [122].

Next, we discuss how the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze in the class ηGx​y=+1\eta_{G_{xy}}=+1 can be mapped to those on the square lattice. To do so, we first implement the geometric mapping between the two lattices as illustrated in Fig. 1(c). Beginning with the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, we have to include two additional symmetry-inequivalent diagonal interactions, denoted by orange and light-green bonds, with coupling strengths Jd′J^{\prime}_{d} and J□J_{\square}, respectively. This introduces six new mean-field amplitudes ud1,…,ud6u_{d_{1}},\ldots,u_{d_{6}}, as shown in Fig. 8(c). The full Ansatz can, in fact, be defined in terms of four fields: usu_{s}, on the NN square bonds; udu_{d}, on the diagonal bonds already present on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice; ud′u_{d^{\prime}}, on the other diagonal bonds in the same set of plaquettes as udu_{d}; and u□u_{\square}, on both diagonals of the empty Shastry-Sutherland plaquettes. The structure of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze with p​4​gp4g symmetry on these reference bonds is then given by

ud′=ud1=ud2=ι˙​χd′0​τ0+Δd′1​τx+Δd′2​τy+χd′3​τz,\displaystyle u_{d^{\prime}}=u_{d_{1}}=u_{d_{2}}=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{d^{\prime}}\tau^{0}+\Delta^{1}_{d^{\prime}}\tau^{x}+\Delta^{2}_{d^{\prime}}\tau^{y}+\chi^{3}_{d^{\prime}}\tau^{z}, (43)
u□=ud3=(τz)p​ud4​(τz)p=(τz)p​ud5​(τz)p=ud6,\displaystyle u_{\square}=u_{d_{3}}=(\tau^{z})^{p}u_{d_{4}}(\tau^{z})^{p}=(\tau^{z})^{p}u_{d_{5}}(\tau^{z})^{p}=u_{d_{6}}, (44)

where

u□≡ι˙​χ□0​τ0+Δ□1​τx+Δ□2​τy+χ□3​τz.u_{\square}\equiv\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{\square}\tau^{0}+\Delta^{1}_{\square}\tau^{x}+\Delta^{2}_{\square}\tau^{y}+\chi^{3}_{\square}\tau^{z}. (45)

The mean-field parameters usu_{s}, udu_{d}, ud′u_{d^{\prime}}, and u□u_{\square} are listed in Table 5. Note that, due to the inclusion of all diagonal bonds, the different signs of ηGx​Tx\eta_{G_{x}T_{x}} are no longer related by gauge transformations.

In general, udu_{d}, ud′u_{d^{\prime}}, and u□u_{\square} are not related by symmetry. However, in the square-lattice limit (after including σx\sigma_{x}), i.e., Jd=Jd′=J□J_{d}=J^{\prime}_{d}=J_{\square}, all diagonal bonds do become symmetry equivalent. This allows us to construct ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze on the square lattice starting from the ones on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. For example, consider the Ansatz labeled Z3000 and PSG 3(c) with ηGx​Tx=−ησx​Gx=+1\eta_{G_{x}T_{x}}=-\eta_{\sigma_{x}G_{x}}=+1 in Table 12. After imposing the constraints associated with σx\sigma_{x}, we obtain the following Ansatz:

u12=u21=u43=u34=χs​τz+Δs​τx,\displaystyle u_{12}=u_{21}=u_{43}=u_{34}=\chi_{s}\tau^{z}+\Delta_{s}\tau^{x}, (46a)
u14=u41=u23=u32=χs​τz−Δs​τx,\displaystyle u_{14}=u_{41}=u_{23}=u_{32}=\chi_{s}\tau^{z}-\Delta_{s}\tau^{x}, (46b)
u13=u42=ud1=ud2=χd​τz,aγ​(u)=0,\displaystyle u_{13}=u_{42}=u_{d_{1}}=u_{d_{2}}=\chi_{d}\tau^{z},\;a_{\gamma}(u)=0, (46c)
ud3=ud4=ud5=ud6=−χd​τz.\displaystyle u_{d_{3}}=u_{d_{4}}=u_{d_{5}}=u_{d_{6}}=-\chi_{d}\tau^{z}. (46d)

It is straightforward to see that after a gauge transformation W⁡(m,n,u)={ι˙​τy,−1,−ι˙​τy,1}W(m,n,u)=\{\dot{\iota}\tau^{y},-1,-\dot{\iota}\tau^{y},1\}, this can be re-expressed as (note that this transformation rotates the nearest-neighbor link field by π/2\pi/2 in the (τz,τx)(\tau^{z},\tau^{x}) plane, so that the amplitudes multiplying τz\tau^{z} and τx\tau^{x} are interchanged on those bonds, while the diagonal bonds are unaffected):

u12=u21=u43=u34=Δs​τz−χs​τx,\displaystyle u_{12}=u_{21}=u_{43}=u_{34}=\Delta_{s}\tau^{z}-\chi_{s}\tau^{x}, (47a)
u14=u41=u23=u32=Δs​τz+χs​τx,\displaystyle u_{14}=u_{41}=u_{23}=u_{32}=\Delta_{s}\tau^{z}+\chi_{s}\tau^{x}, (47b)
u13=ud2=ud3=ud5=χd​τz,aγ​(u)=0,\displaystyle u_{13}=u_{d_{2}}=u_{d_{3}}=u_{d_{5}}=\chi_{d}\tau^{z},\;a_{\gamma}(u)=0, (47c)
u42=ud1=ud4=ud6=−χd​τz.\displaystyle u_{42}=u_{d_{1}}=u_{d_{4}}=u_{d_{6}}=-\chi_{d}\tau^{z}. (47d)

In the canonical square-lattice Cartesian notation, it can be written as

u𝐱^\displaystyle u_{\mathbf{\hat{x}}} =Δs​τz−χs​τx,u𝐲^=Δs​τz+χs​τx,\displaystyle=\Delta_{s}\tau^{z}-\chi_{s}\tau^{x},\;u_{\mathbf{\hat{y}}}=\Delta_{s}\tau^{z}+\chi_{s}\tau^{x}, (48a)
u𝐱^+𝐲^\displaystyle u_{\mathbf{\hat{x}}+\mathbf{\hat{y}}} =χd​τz,u−𝐱^+𝐲^=−χd​τz,aγ​(u)=0.\displaystyle=\chi_{d}\tau^{z},\;u_{\mathbf{-\hat{x}}+\mathbf{\hat{y}}}=-\chi_{d}\tau^{z},\;a_{\gamma}(u)=0. (48b)

This corresponds to the Z2Az​zzz13 Ansatz in the PSG classification by Wen [122]. Thus, the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansatz Z3000 on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice can be continuously connected to the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansatz Z2Az​zzz13 on the square lattice. This connection is protected by the projective realization of GxG_{x} and σx​y\sigma_{xy}. When considering up to NNN amplitudes, among the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze listed in this work, five more can be realized with IGG ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, which are labeled Z2A0013, Z2B0013, Z2Ax​xxx0zz, Z2Axx2(12)nn, and Z2Bxx2(12)nn. Their connections to the square lattice can be established following a procedure similar to that carried out above for the Z2Az​zzz13 Ansatz, as summarized in Table 6.

V Numerical Results

Unless stated otherwise, all the results of this section and of Sec. VI refer to the pure Shastry-Sutherland model, i.e., to 𝒥≡Jd′=J□=0\mathcal{J}\equiv J^{\prime}_{d}=J_{\square}=0 in Eq. (2), so that Js/JdJ_{s}/J_{d} is the only tuning parameter. The single exception is Fig. 18, where 𝒥\mathcal{J} is varied in order to follow the river of liquidity toward the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} limit; there, the value of 𝒥/Js\mathcal{J}/J_{s} is quoted explicitly for every data point.

V.1 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac state: Mean-field properties

Given that the gapless Z3000 state serves as the most promising candidate to describe the QSL in the generalized SSM (as we will show below), we now present its corresponding variational wavefunction in terms of Abrikosov pseudo-fermions [1]. First, we define a mean-field state in the fermionic Hilbert space by taking the ground state |ϕMF⟩|\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\rm MF}\rangle of the following noninteracting spinon Hamiltonian, which is of the generalized Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer form:

ℋ^\displaystyle{\cal\hat{H}} Z3000MF=χd∑⟨i​j⟩teal,αsdi​jf^i,α†f^j,α+χd′∑⟨i​j⟩orange,αsd′i​jf^i,α†f^j,α{}^{\text{Z3000}}_{{\rm MF}}=\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{d}\hskip-5.69046pt\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{\text{teal}},\alpha}{\rm s}^{d}_{ij}\hat{f}_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\alpha}+\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{d^{\prime}}\hskip-5.69046pt\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{\text{orange}},\alpha}{\rm s}^{d^{\prime}}_{ij}\hat{f}_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\alpha}
+∑⟨i​j⟩blue[χs∑αsi​jsf^i,α†f^j,α+Δsνi​js(f^i,↑†f^j,↓†+h.c.)]\displaystyle+\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{\text{blue}}}\,\,\left[\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}\sum_{\alpha}{\rm s}^{s}_{ij}\hat{f}_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\alpha}+\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}{\nu}^{s}_{ij}\big(\hat{f}_{i,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{j,\downarrow}+{\rm h.c.}\big)\right]
+∑⟨i​j⟩green[χ□∑αsi​j□f^i,α†f^j,α+Δ□νi​j□(f^i,↑†f^j,↓†+h.c.)]\displaystyle+\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{\text{green}}}\left[\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\square}\sum_{\alpha}{\rm s}^{\square}_{ij}\hat{f}_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\alpha}+\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\square}{\nu}^{\square}_{ij}\big(\hat{f}_{i,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{j,\downarrow}+{\rm h.c.}\big)\right]
+μ∑i,αf^i,α†f^i,α.\displaystyle+\mu\sum_{i,\alpha}\hat{f}_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\alpha}\,. (49)

Here, si​j{\rm s}_{ij} and νi​j\nu_{ij} are sign factors for hoppings and pairings, respectively, which take values +1​(−1)+1(-1) for bonds marked as solid (dashed) in Fig. 10(b); all the bond sums run over ordered pairs (i,j)(i,j), so that every term above is Hermitian and the pairing is a spin singlet. The different colors in Fig. 10(b) label the symmetry-inequivalent bonds, as referenced in Eq. (49). We fix χs=1\chi_{s}=1 as the overall energy scale, and the resulting wavefunction is thus parametrized by six variational parameters: χd\chi_{d}, χd′\chi_{d^{\prime}}, χ□\chi_{\square}, Δs\Delta_{s}, Δ□\Delta_{\square}, and the onsite chemical potential, μ\mu.

Although the Z3000 Ansatz can be obtained by lowering the U(1) IGG—via singlet pairing terms—of three distinct U(1) states, namely, U100, U300, and U800 in Table 4, it is most straightforward to view it as a descendant of the parent U100 state (see also App. I). Indeed, because symmetries are realized linearly (nonprojectively) in the U100 state, this state allows for uniform real hopping amplitudes on all diagonal and square-lattice bonds. Thus, it can be retrieved from the Z3000 Ansatz (49) by setting the pairings Δs=Δ□=0\Delta_{s}=\Delta_{\square}=0. The band structure of the parent U100 state is shown in Fig. 11(a), and, at half filling, it features a Fermi surface [Fig. 11(b)]. On adding a nonzero Δs\Delta_{s}, the nearly square-shaped Fermi surface surrounding the Γ\Gamma point is completely gapped out, and the other Fermi surfaces in the vicinity of the MM (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi/2) points shrink to isolated points, forming Dirac cones at M⁡(π/2,π/2)+(±ε,±ε)M(\pi/2,\pi/2)+(\pm\varepsilon,\pm\varepsilon). The Dirac points always reside on the line Γ​M¯\overline{\Gamma M}. This is illustrated in Fig. 33 [App. F], where we show the contour plot of the energies of the lowest eigenmode of Z3000 in the kxk_{x}–kyk_{y} plane. The dependence of the magnitude of ε\varepsilon on all the variational parameters is illustrated in Fig. 34 [App. F]. In Fig. 12(a), we plot the dispersion of the Z3000 state for the VMC-optimized parameters at Js/Jd=0.8J_{s}/J_{d}=0.8 while the four Dirac cones surrounding the MM point are shown in Fig. 12(b). We also present the spin correlations of this mean-field state, as reflected in its dynamical and equal-time spin structure factors, in Figs. 12(c) and (d), respectively.

It is worthwhile to discuss the splitting of the Dirac nodes in the Z3000 Ansatz, particularly in comparison with those in the Z2Az​zzz13 state on the square lattice [122]. When one considers only uniform hopping χs\chi_{s} and dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} pairing Δs\Delta_{s} on the nearest-neighbor bonds33 3 One can additionally include pairing on the third-nearest-neighbor bonds (which are twice the nearest-neighbor distance), i.e., connecting (0,0)(0,0) to (±2,0)(\pm 2,0) and (0,±2)(0,\pm 2)., both the square and Shastry-Sutherland lattices exhibit Dirac nodes at the commensurate momenta M(±π/2,±π/2)M(\pm{\pi}/{2},\pm{\pi}/{2}) [see Figs. 11(c) and 11(d)]. However, the inclusion of any of the additional hopping amplitudes χd\chi_{d}, χd′\chi_{d^{\prime}}, χ□\chi_{\square}, or of the onsite term μ\mu in the Z3000 Ansatz splits the Dirac node at each MM point into four nodes residing at incommensurate momenta (±π/2±ε,±π/2±ε)(\pm{\pi}/{2}\pm\varepsilon,\pm{\pi}/{2}\pm\varepsilon), with the nodes always located along Γ​M¯\overline{\Gamma M} [marked by blue dots in Fig. 11(d)]. The node positions can in fact be obtained in closed form: as shown in App. G, the gapless points are the zeros of a quartic polynomial whose coefficients are explicit functions of all the mean-field amplitudes. In particular, the nodes remain exactly commensurate, ε=0\varepsilon=0, if and only if μ=±(χd+χd′−2​χ□)\mu=\pm(\chi_{d}+\chi_{d^{\prime}}-2\chi_{\square}), independently of Δs\Delta_{s} and Δ□\Delta_{\square}; the empty-square pairing Δ□\Delta_{\square} acting alone leaves the nodes pinned at MM. Thus, the Z3000 state can also be viewed as descending from the U800 Ansatz. We illustrate this behavior using a contour plot of the lowest-energy eigenmode of the Z3000 state, shown in Fig. 12(e).

A similar phenomenon occurs in the square-lattice Z2Az​zzz13 state: including additional mean-field amplitudes corresponding to dx​yd_{xy} pairings on the diagonals of the squares shifts the Dirac nodes from (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm{\pi}/{2},\pm{\pi}/{2}) to ±(π/2+ε,π/2+ε)\pm({\pi}/{2}+\varepsilon,{\pi}/{2}+\varepsilon) and ±(−π/2+ε,π/2−ε)\pm(-{\pi}/{2}+\varepsilon,{\pi}/{2}-\varepsilon), as shown in Fig. 12(f). In this case, the band structure exhibits C4C_{4} symmetry about (π,0)(\pi,0) and (0,π)(0,\pi), and C2C_{2} symmetry about (0,0)(0,0). Therefore, although the Z3000 and Z2Az​zzz13 Ansätze are adiabatically connected, the equivalence of their band structures is not immediately apparent. The origin of this difference lies in the gauge structure: the Z2Az​zzz13 Ansatz in Ref. [122] is defined in the geometrical unit cell, whereas the Z3000 Ansatz is realized in a 2×22\times 2 unit cell. To facilitate a direct comparison, we redefine the Z2Az​zzz13 Ansatz in a 2×22\times 2 unit cell and back-fold the Brillouin zone accordingly. This procedure leads to an identical splitting of Dirac nodes in the spinon dispersion of the lowest eigenmode [see Fig. 12(g)], as observed for the Z3000 state. Consequently, one expects the gapless points in the spin excitations to appear at (π±δ,π±δ)(\pi\pm\delta,\pi\pm\delta) (where δ=2​ε\delta=2\varepsilon), as well as at (π,±δ)(\pi,\pm\delta) and (±δ,π)(\pm\delta,\pi), consistent with the two-spinon excitation spectra of the Z2Az​zzz13 state reported in Ref. [122]. Signatures of these gapless excitations are already visible in the mean-field dynamical structure factor shown in Fig. 12(c). They become more pronounced beyond the mean-field level upon including gauge fluctuations, as will be demonstrated in the dynamical structure factor obtained from Keldysh pf-FRG.

It is also instructive to compare these results with previous studies of the Z2Az​zzz13 state on the square lattice, which has been proposed as a candidate QSL ground state of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model in Refs. [34, 25]. In those works, a version of the Z2Az​zzz13 Ansatz modified relative to the original proposal in Ref. [122] is adopted in order to realize the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge structure. Specifically, the dx​yd_{xy} pairing is defined on bonds connecting (0,0)(0,0) to (±2,±2)(\pm 2,\pm 2)—which are twice the length of the diagonals inside the squares, corresponding to the fifth-nearest-neighbor bonds—instead of the bonds connecting (0,0)(0,0) to (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1), i.e., the diagonals inside the squares as originally considered in Ref. [122]. Restricting the dx​yd_{xy} singlet pairing amplitudes to the (±2,±2)(\pm 2,\pm 2) bonds ensures that the Dirac points remain located at the commensurate momenta (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm{\pi}/{2},\pm{\pi}/{2}) in the mean-field spectrum. As a consequence, the two-spinon excitation spectrum contains gapless excitations at (π,π)(\pi,\pi), (π,0)(\pi,0), and (0,π)(0,\pi), rather than at the incommensurate points (π±δ,π±δ)(\pi\pm\delta,\pi\pm\delta), (π,±δ)(\pi,\pm\delta), and (±δ,π)(\pm\delta,\pi) that would arise if the dx​yd_{xy} pairings were defined on the (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1) bonds (see Ref. [122]).

On the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, however, we find that it is not possible to define the Z2Az​zzz13 Ansatz in an analogous gauge that preserves the Dirac points at (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm{\pi}/{2},\pm{\pi}/{2}). Indeed, even when the singlet pairing Δ□\Delta_{\square} is restricted to the (±2,±2)(\pm 2,\pm 2) diagonals of the empty squares—rather than the (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1) diagonals—each Dirac point at (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm{\pi}/{2},\pm{\pi}/{2}) still splits into four nodes located at (±π/2±ε,±π/2±ε)(\pm{\pi}/{2}\pm\varepsilon,\pm{\pi}/{2}\pm\varepsilon). As a result, the gapless points in the spin excitation spectrum appear at the same incommensurate momenta (π±δ,π±δ)(\pi\pm\delta,\pi\pm\delta), (π,±δ)(\pi,\pm\delta), and (±δ,π)(\pm\delta,\pi) as discussed in Ref. [122], with δ=2​ε\delta=2\varepsilon (see App. G for the exact values of ε\varepsilon). This behavior is manifest in the mean-field dynamical spin structure factor of Fig. 12(c); the Keldysh pf-FRG result of Fig. 20(a) is consistent with it, although the small values of δ\delta obtained here lie below the momentum resolution of the lattices accessible to pf-FRG.

Therefore, to construct an Ansatz that naturally interpolates between the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model and the Shastry-Sutherland geometry, we use the short-range representative of the Z2Az​zzz13 PSG introduced in Ref. [122], with dx​yd_{xy} pairings on the (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1) diagonals. This choice produces split Dirac nodes and low-frequency spin excitations at incommensurate momenta. It should be distinguished from the square-lattice variational representative of Ref. [34], in which the dx​yd_{xy} pairing is placed on fifth-nearest-neighbor (±2,±2)(\pm 2,\pm 2) bonds; that representative keeps the Dirac nodes pinned at (±π/2,±π/2)(\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi/2) and gives the lower variational energy on the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} axis. Away from this high-symmetry limit, however, the fifth-neighbor pairing does not give a detectable energy gain in the Shastry-Sutherland geometry, while the short-range representative is energetically preferred in our optimized Gutzwiller-projected calculations. The two wavefunctions are therefore distinct microscopic representatives of the same Z2Az​zzz13/Z3000 PSG class, rather than gauge-equivalent forms of a single Ansatz.

After performing a particle-hole transformation on the spinons with flavor ↓\downarrow,

f^i,↓†→f^i,↓,f^i,↑†→f^i,↑†,\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i,\downarrow}\to\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\downarrow},\quad\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i,\uparrow}\to\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i,\uparrow}, (50)

the mean-field Hamiltonian (49) commutes with the total number of particles. Thus, |ϕMF⟩|\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\rm MF}\rangle is defined by filling suitable single-particle orbitals. In this process, the boundary conditions should be chosen so that they lead to a unique state (by filling all orbitals in a shell with the same mean-field energy). Periodic (P) and antiperiodic (A) boundary conditions along the 𝐚1{\bf a}_{1} and 𝐚2{\bf a}_{2} lattice-vector directions [see Fig. 1(b)] can be considered, leading to four choices: [P,P], [P,A], [A,P], and [A,A]. Here, for the Z3000 state, we impose antiperiodic and periodic boundary conditions along the 𝐚1{\bf a}_{1} and 𝐚2{\bf a}_{2} directions, respectively, i.e., [A,P], which leads to a closed shell (unique state) on L×LL\times L clusters with any even LL.

V.2 Gutzwiller-projected Ansatz

A legitimate QSL wavefunction, residing in the correct sector with one fermion per site (corresponding to the physical Hilbert space of the spin-1/21/2 model), is then obtained by applying the Gutzwiller projector to the mean-field state |ϕMF⟩|\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\rm MF}\rangle:

|ΨQSL⟩=𝒫G​|ϕMF⟩,|\Psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\rm QSL}}\rangle={\cal P}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\text{G}}|\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\rm MF}\rangle\,, (51)

where 𝒫G=∏i(n^i,↑−n^i,↓)2{\cal P}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\text{G}}=\prod_{i}\big(\hat{n}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\uparrow}-\hat{n}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\downarrow}\big)^{2}, n^i,α=f^i,α†​f^i,α\hat{n}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\alpha}=\hat{f}_{i,\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\alpha} being the fermionic density of flavor α\alpha on site ii. The variational energy and correlation functions for |ΨQSL⟩|\Psi_{{\rm QSL}}\rangle can be computed in a straightforward fashion using Monte Carlo sampling, by virtue of which the constraint is imposed exactly [7]. Furthermore, a stochastic reconfiguration (SR) optimization enables us to obtain accurate estimates of the variational parameters contained in Eq. (49) with small statistical uncertainties [111, 135], even when a large number of parameters are involved [43, 40, 33, 26, 85].

A standard technique to systematically improve the accuracy of variational wavefunctions and approach the true ground state involves the application of a few Lánczos steps on a given variational state |ΨQSL⟩|\Psi_{\rm QSL}\rangle [110, 6]:

|Ψp​-​LS⟩=(1+∑k=1pλk​ℋ^k)​|ΨQSL⟩,|\Psi_{p\text{-}\rm{LS}}\rangle=\left(1+\sum_{k=1}^{p}\lambda_{k}{\cal\hat{H}}^{k}\right)|\Psi_{{\rm QSL}}\rangle\,, (52)

where the λk\lambda_{k}s are variational parameters. For large enough pp, |Ψp​-​LS⟩|\Psi_{p\text{-}\rm{LS}}\rangle is guaranteed to converge to the exact ground state |Ψex⟩|\Psi_{\rm ex}\rangle provided the initial trial state |ΨQSL⟩|\Psi_{\rm QSL}\rangle is not orthogonal to |Ψex⟩|\Psi_{\rm ex}\rangle, i.e., for ⟨Ψex|ΨQSL⟩≠0\langle\Psi_{\rm ex}|\Psi_{\rm QSL}\rangle\neq 0. However, on large clusters, only a few Lánczos steps can be efficiently executed, and here, we consider the cases p=1p=1 and p=2p=2 (p=0p=0 corresponds to the initial trial wavefunction |ΨQSL⟩|\Psi_{\rm QSL}\rangle). Based on this sequence, an estimate of the exact ground-state energy can be obtained by the method of zero-variance extrapolation. In fact, for sufficiently accurate states, E−Eex≈constant×σ2E-E_{\rm ex}\approx{\rm constant}\times\sigma^{2}, where E=⟨ℋ^⟩/NE=\langle{\cal\hat{H}}\rangle/N and σ2=(⟨ℋ^2⟩−⟨ℋ^⟩2)/N\sigma^{2}=(\langle{\cal\hat{H}}^{2}\rangle{-}\langle{\cal\hat{H}}\rangle^{2})/N are the energy and variance per site, respectively. Thus, the exact ground-state energy EexE_{\rm ex} can be extracted by fitting EE vs σ2\sigma^{2} for p=0p=0, 11, and 22. The energy, its variance, and the correlation functions after the application of a few Lánczos steps are calculated using the standard variational Monte Carlo method.
